lessonTitle: Quality Management Systems: PDCA, CAPA and Pareto Analysis

blocks.text: A machining line scraps 275 parts in a month. Management wants to fix 'quality', but quality is not one problem: it is oversize bores, scratches, burrs, damaged threads, wrong markings, each with a different cause. A quality management system gives a disciplined way to decide which problem to attack first, how to fix the cause and not only the symptom, and how to make sure the fix lasts.

blocks.markdown: A **quality management system (QMS)** is the set of policies, processes and records an organisation uses to meet customer and regulatory requirements consistently. The international standard ISO 9001 specifies requirements for a QMS and is built on seven principles: customer focus, leadership, engagement of people, the process approach, improvement, evidence-based decision making and relationship management. Certification shows that a system exists and is followed; it does not by itself guarantee that every part is good.

blocks.title: The plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle
blocks.text: PDCA is a repeating four-step method for improvement. **Plan**: define the problem with data, find the cause and set a measurable target. **Do**: implement the change on a small scale (a pilot). **Check**: measure the results and compare them with the target. **Act**: if the change worked, standardise it (update procedures, train people); if not, revise the plan. Then the cycle repeats at a higher standard.

rows: What is wrong, why, and what is the target?
Bore oversize caused by tool wear; target: fewer than 10 oversize per week
Try the change on a small scale
Change tool every 500 parts instead of 800, on one machine
Did it work? Compare with the target
Oversize drops from 31 to 9 per week on the pilot machine
Revise tool-change interval in the work instruction; roll out; train operators
blocks.caption: PDCA applied to a quality problem.

blocks.title: PDCA on oversize bores
blocks.prompt: Oversize bores average 31 per week. The Plan identifies tool wear, and a Do pilot changes the tool every 500 parts rather than every 800 on one machine. After four weeks the oversize count on that machine averages 9 per week. Assess the result and decide the Act step.

steps.text: Check: compute the reduction against the baseline.
Compare with the target. A 71% reduction brings the weekly count to 9, which meets the plan's goal.

Act: standardise, because the change worked. Update the work instruction, train the operators, extend the new interval to the other machines, and keep monitoring so that the cycle can repeat on the next biggest cause.

blocks.answer: The pilot cut oversize bores by 71%, so the new tool-change interval becomes the standard. The cycle then restarts on the next cause.

blocks.title: Corrective and preventive action (CAPA) records
blocks.text: A **correction** fixes the nonconforming product in front of you (rework, scrap, sort). A **corrective action** removes the cause of an existing nonconformity so that it does not recur. A **preventive action** removes the cause of a potential nonconformity before it happens. A CAPA record documents this: description of the problem, containment, root-cause analysis (for example the 5-whys), the action, owner and due date, verification of effectiveness, and closure. ISO 9001:2015 covers prevention through risk-based thinking rather than a separate clause, but CAPA records are still the usual way of documenting both.

items: Containment limits the damage now (hold stock, inspect 100%).
Root cause analysis asks why until a cause that can be removed is found, not 'operator error'.
The action must address the root cause, with an owner and a date.
Verification of effectiveness checks, after a defined period, that the problem has not recurred; without it a record can be closed while the fault persists.
The record is evidence for audits, customers and future problems.

blocks.markdown: **Pareto charts.** Many problems have a few causes that account for most of the effect (the Pareto principle, roughly 80:20). A Pareto chart sorts categories from the most frequent (or costly) to the least and plots a cumulative percentage line, so the *vital few* causes stand out from the *trivial many*.

blocks.caption: Scrap data for one month (275 parts).

blocks.title: Using the Pareto data
blocks.prompt: Use the table to decide where to start, and what the top three categories give.

steps.text: Total count and the first category's share.
Cumulative share of the top three categories.
Interpretation: three of six categories explain about 80% of the scrap, so effort goes first to oversize bores, then scratches and burrs. The remaining categories are the trivial many.

blocks.answer: Oversize bores alone account for 42.9%, and the top three categories for 81.1%, so these are the priorities.

blocks.title: Count is not cost
blocks.text: A Pareto by frequency can mislead if defects have very different consequences. A rare defect that costs 20 cu to rework may matter more than a common one costing 2 cu. Where costs differ, weight the counts by cost, or by safety impact, before ranking.

points: PDCA: plan with data and a target, do a small pilot, check against the target, then act by standardising or revising.

CAPA: correction treats the product, corrective action removes the cause of an existing problem, preventive action removes the cause of a potential one, and a verification of effectiveness closes the record.
A Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency or cost with a cumulative line, so effort is focused on the vital few; weight by cost when consequences differ.

questions.stem: In the PDCA cycle, a team has introduced a new inspection step on one line and now compares defect rates before and after. Which phase is this?

options.text: Check, because results are being compared with the target
Plan, because the data are being analysed
Do, because the new step is in use
Act, because the new step has been adopted

questions.correctOptionText: Check, because results are being compared with the target

distractorRationale.a: Comparing results with the target after a change is the Check step.
distractorRationale.b: Plan comes before the change; here the change has already been made.
distractorRationale.c: Do is the implementation of the change; the comparison of results is Check.
distractorRationale.d: Act follows Check and standardises or revises the change.

questions.explanation: The sequence is Plan the change, Do it at small scale, Check the results against the target, then Act. Only after the comparison can the team decide whether to adopt the change.

questions.stem: A batch of valve bodies with undersize bores is reworked by re-boring. Separately, the team traces the problem to a worn boring bar and changes the tool-change interval. How are these two actions classified?

options.text: Re-boring is a correction, and the interval change is a corrective action
Re-boring is a corrective action, and the interval change is a correction
Both are corrective actions, because both stop defects
Both are preventive actions, because both avoid scrap

questions.correctOptionText: Re-boring is a correction, and the interval change is a corrective action

distractorRationale.a: Fixing the parts is a correction; removing the cause is a corrective action.
distractorRationale.b: The cause is removed by the interval change, so that is the corrective action.
distractorRationale.c: Correction fixes the product; corrective action fixes the cause.
distractorRationale.d: The defect has already occurred, so the first is a correction and the second a corrective action.

questions.explanation: A correction treats the nonconforming product, while a corrective action targets the root cause so that the problem does not recur. Both are normally recorded in the CAPA record, along with the verification.

questions.stem: Why does a CAPA record require a verification-of-effectiveness step before it is closed?

options.text: To assign blame to the operator responsible
To prove the audit was carried out on time
To record the cost of the rework
To confirm, with data after a set period, that the problem has not recurred and the action worked

questions.correctOptionText: To confirm, with data after a set period, that the problem has not recurred and the action worked

distractorRationale.a: A CAPA is about the system and the cause, not blame.
distractorRationale.b: Verification concerns the effect of the action, not the audit schedule.
distractorRationale.c: Cost can be recorded, but verification is about whether the fix worked.
distractorRationale.d: Verification shows by evidence that the action removed the cause.

questions.explanation: Without it a record could be closed on the assumption that the action worked. Checking the defect rate after a defined period turns the assumption into evidence.

questions.stem: What does a Pareto chart of defect causes show?

options.text: Causes sorted from largest to smallest with a cumulative percentage line, to identify the vital few
The change in a process mean over time with control limits
The relationship between two variables as a scatter of points
The causes of a problem as branches from a central spine

questions.correctOptionText: Causes sorted from largest to smallest with a cumulative percentage line, to identify the vital few

distractorRationale.a: A Pareto chart ranks categories and shows their cumulative share.
distractorRationale.b: That describes a control chart, not a Pareto chart.

questions.explanation: By ordering categories from largest to smallest and adding the cumulative percentage, a Pareto chart shows which few categories account for most of the effect. Effort is then focused where it will pay most.

questions.stem: Defect A occurs 100 times a month and costs 2 cu per occurrence. Defect B occurs 30 times a month and costs 20 cu per occurrence. Which should be prioritised and why?

options.text: Defect B, because its monthly cost of 600 cu exceeds the 200 cu of A
Defect A, because it is the most frequent
Defect A, because 100 is greater than 30
Neither, because cost differences do not matter

questions.correctOptionText: Defect B, because its monthly cost of 600 cu exceeds the 200 cu of A

distractorRationale.a: Monthly cost is $100\times2=200$ cu for A and $30\times20=600$ cu for B.
distractorRationale.b: Frequency alone ignores that each B costs ten times as much.
distractorRationale.c: The count ranking is the trap; cost ranking reverses it.
distractorRationale.d: Cost-weighted ranking is the correct way to prioritise when consequences differ.

questions.explanation: A frequency Pareto puts A first, but weighting by cost puts B first at three times the cost. This is why Pareto charts should use cost or severity when the consequences differ.

questions.stem: A weld inspection log shows porosity 52, undercut 31, spatter 22, cracks 9 and other 6 defects. Calculate the cumulative percentage of defects accounted for by the top two categories.
questions.explanation: The total is $52+31+22+9+6=120$. The top two categories sum to $52+31=83$, which is $83/120=0.692$, or 69.2%.

questions.stem: After a pilot change in a PDCA cycle, weekly defects fell from 48 to 30. Calculate the percentage reduction.
questions.explanation: The reduction is $(48-30)/48=18/48=0.375$, so 37.5%. This value is compared with the target set in the Plan step.

questions.stem: A corrective action is expected to eliminate 85% of 240 scrapped parts per year, each costing 18.50 cu. Calculate the annual saving in cu.
questions.explanation: The parts saved are $0.85\times240=204$ per year. At 18.50 cu each, the saving is $204\times18.50=3774$ cu.

questions.stem: A recurring complaint concerns scratched surfaces on a pump housing. Describe how you would apply PDCA to the problem, and what a CAPA record for it should contain. Include the difference between correction and corrective action, and how you would show that the action worked.
markingGuide: Plan: collect data on scratches, locate where they occur, find the root cause (for example the 5-whys), set a measurable target
Do: pilot the change, for example a protective fixture or handling change on one line
Check: compare scratch rate with the target
Act: standardise if effective, update procedures and train; otherwise replan
CAPA record: problem description, containment, root cause, action, owner, due date, verification, closure
Correction = rework or scrap of the scratched housings; corrective action = removing the cause; verification by data after a period
questions.explanation: PDCA organises the work: plan from data, pilot the change, check it against the target and standardise if it works. The CAPA record documents the correction, the root cause, the corrective action, its owner and the evidence, collected after a set period, that the scratches no longer recur.

questions.stem: A hydraulic test line records 100 leaks in a month: seal damage 46, thread burrs 28, porosity 17, wrong torque 5, other 4. Build the cumulative percentages, identify the vital few, and explain how you would test whether frequency is the right basis for ranking. Give one limitation of a Pareto analysis.
markingGuide: Vital few: seal damage and thread burrs (74%); porosity brings the total to 91%
Check cost or severity weighting, since frequency may not reflect consequences (rank by cost per occurrence times count)
Limitation: shows where the problem is, not the cause; it depends on how categories are defined; it is a snapshot
Notes a follow-up Pareto after the fix to confirm improvement
questions.explanation: The cumulative shares are 46%, 74%, 91%, 96% and 100%, so seal damage and thread burrs are the vital few, accounting for 74% of leaks. Ranking should be checked against cost or severity, and a Pareto chart only shows where to look, not why the failures occur.
